evidence.excerpt: An external contract can take over control flow and call back before the first function invocation finishes. Remediation: perform internal state changes before the external call, using checks-effects-interactions, or use a reentrancy lock. A lock blocks the unwanted callback into the protected path; it does not prevent control passing to the external callee.
evidence.source_quote:
One of the major dangers of calling external contracts is that they can take over the control flow. In the reentrancy attack (a.k.a. recursive call attack), a malicious contract calls back into the calling contract before the first invocation of the function is finished. This may cause the different invocations of the function to interact in undesirable ways.

## Remediation

The best practices to avoid Reentrancy weaknesses are:

- Make sure all internal state changes are performed before the call is executed. This is known as the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern
- Use a reentrancy lock (ie. OpenZeppelin's ReentrancyGuard).

evidence.excerpt: Low-level calls return a success value. A low-level call may fail and return false while the caller continues. Ignoring that return value can leave contract accounting inconsistent because the caller may record an operation as successful when the call failed.
evidence.source_quote: Description The return value of a message call is not checked. Execution will resume even if the called contract throws an exception. If the call fails accidentally or an attacker forces the call to fail, this may cause unexpected behaviour in the subsequent program logic. Remediation If you choose to use low-level call methods, make sure to handle the possibility that the call will fail by checking the return value.

evidence.excerpt: Missing access restrictions on functions that transfer ether can allow arbitrary users to withdraw funds. Implement controls so withdrawals can only be triggered by authorized parties. The source's sample access control checks msg.sender against a stored creator or owner and uses an onlyOwner modifier.
evidence.source_quote: Description Due to missing or insufficient access controls, malicious parties can withdraw some or all Ether from the contract account. This bug is sometimes caused by unintentionally exposing initialization functions. By wrongly naming a function intended to be a constructor, the constructor code ends up in the runtime byte code and can be called by anyone to re-initialize the contract. Remediation Implement controls so withdrawals can only be triggered by authorized parties or according to the specs of the smart contract system.

It will make available the modifier onlyOwner, which can be applied to your functions to restrict their use to the owner.

evidence.excerpt: Price oracle manipulation exploits weaknesses in price feeds to distort contract logic; validate inputs and use resilient oracle sources.
evidence.source_quote: Description ¶ Price Oracle manipulation refers to the exploitation of vulnerabilities in price oracles to manipulate contract logic. This can lead to: - Unauthorized actions by malicious actors. - Loss of funds or data. - Exploitation of the contract's logic. Remediation ¶ Use decentralized oracles: Leverage multiple decentralized oracles for price data. Validate inputs: Ensure all oracle data is properly validated before use.
evidence.scope: Use the documented oracle conditions and threat model

evidence.excerpt: Aggregate multiple price sources. Use time-weighted averages (TWAPs) over sufficient windows to resist short-lived manipulations. Reject prices older than a maximum staleness threshold.
evidence.source_quote: Aggregate multiple sources : Use median/mean of several DEXs / oracles. Reject outliers and anomalous deviations. Time-based defenses : Use TWAPs over sufficient windows to resist short-lived manipulations. Reject prices older than a maximum staleness threshold. Liquidity-aware design : Avoid basing core prices on illiquid pools . Cap impact of a single pool/feed on global pricing. Fail-safe behavior : On suspicious or unavailable data, halt sensitive operations (borrowing, liquidations). Use circuit breakers and rate limiting on parameter changes. Monitoring & alerting : Track price deviations between your oracle and reference markets. Set automated alerts for out-of-band movements or stuck oracles.
evidence.scope: Use the documented oracle conditions and threat model

To mitigate this risk, contracts should aggregate multiple oracle and DEX price sources while rejecting anomalous outlier deviations.
Complementary protection includes using Time-Weighted Average Prices (TWAPs) over sufficient windows and rejecting stale prices beyond maximum thresholds.
Implement fail-safe behaviors that halt sensitive operations like borrowing or liquidations when oracle data is suspicious or unavailable.

evidence.excerpt: A failing external call can revert a wider transaction and prevent progress for other participants.
evidence.source_quote: Description External calls can fail accidentally or deliberately, which can cause a DoS condition in the contract. To minimize the damage caused by such failures, it is better to isolate each external call into its own transaction that can be initiated by the recipient of the call. This is especially relevant for payments, where it is better to let users withdraw funds rather than push funds to them automatically (this also reduces the chance of problems with the gas limit). Remediation It is recommended to follow call best practices: Avoid combining multiple calls in a single transaction, especially when calls are executed as part of a loop Always assume that external calls can fail Implement the contract logic to handle failed calls
